articles.title_orig: Putin floats meeting with U.S. and China on ending war in Ukraine
articles.title_zh: Putin floats meeting with U.S. and China on ending war in Ukraine
articles.content_orig:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has reportedly floated a three-way summit between himself, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping to negotiate an end to the war in Ukraine, without Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy at the table.
The meeting was mentioned in a phone call to Trump on Oct. 9, the Wall Street Journal reported on Monday, citing a former Russian intelligence officer briefed on the matter. Such a summit may take place at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in November in the Chinese city of Shenzhen, according to the report.
The call also produced a deal for Moscow to sell diesel on the global market.
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said early Monday that "there's been talks of a meeting. I don't know whether it's been finalized, but the president has been clear," he said in comments reported by Reuters.
"The president is open to anything that he can do to help bring a war to an end, if it's possible, and we'll continue to look for opportunities to do that," Rubio told reporters during a visit to Uzbekistan.
It comes amid mounting tensions between Ukraine and the U.S., its largest military backer. Over the past week, a series of moves by the Trump administration has raised fresh questions about Washington's reliability as Kyiv's most important military partner. It caused alarm among European allies and prompted criticism from fellow Republicans.
Over the weekend, Trump defended his decision to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports, as well as an executive order on Oct. 18 to waive new Russia sanctions from a bill introduced by the late Senator Lindsey Graham.
Trump and Zelenskyy have traded criticism over how to end the war in Ukraine, with Trump accusing the Ukrainian president of not wanting peace , while Zelenskyy has argued that Washington's easing of sanctions on Russia risks prolonging the conflict. In a post on X, Zelenskyy said that ″the decision to undo all of this, to block all of it, seems wrong to me."
The tensions come as Russia launched another wave of overnight attacks on Ukraine, firing 16 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region and more than 200 drones across the country, according to Zelenskyy.
In a post on X on Monday, Zelenskyy said the strikes damaged more than 10 energy infrastructure facilities, leaving at least 550,000 households without power. He also said Ukraine had once again received no advance warning from its partners about the missile attacks. Casualties were reported, while a medical clinic, school, metro station and residential buildings were also damaged.
Ukraine's First Deputy Minister for Recovery, Infrastructure and Transport Serhiy Derkach told CNBC on Monday that Kyiv still hoped to retain Washington's support despite the growing tensions.
Asked whether the Trump administration was abandoning Ukraine and siding with Russia, Derkach said he did not believe the U.S. was abandoning Kyiv, but stressed that Ukraine hoped Washington would continue helping it or at least "stay in the middle."
"That's most important for us actually, not to lose the support of the U.S.," he said.
Russia has also intensified attacks on Ukraine's transport infrastructure, including road border crossings, railways and shipping routes, Derkach said.
It comes after Trump told Ukraine to stop striking Russian energy infrastructure, claiming that it was driving up global diesel prices.
Despite an "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump on Oct. 11, Russia continued striking Ukrainian infrastructure. Kyiv paused its attacks for three days before resuming them last Thursday, citing continued Russian strikes.
"America should see that Russia is not taking any reciprocal steps in response to sanctions relief or agreements. On the contrary, they take every signal of an opportunity to make money as proof that their bet on war is paying off and they can keep fighting," the Ukrainian president wrote on Sunday.
On Sunday, he also told Bloomberg that "steps have been taken to convince Ukraine to capitulate."
"I am not saying that this is the goal our partners are pursuing. I don't want to think that our American partners believe the war" against Russia "could be ended sooner at Ukraine's expense. But that's how it looks."
Over the weekend, both Kyiv and Moscow traded strikes, with Ukraine launching a strike of over 1,000 drones into Russia, setting fires at an oil export terminal and refinery in the city of St. Petersburg, while Moscow pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles.
Last week, Kyiv also accused Washington of ordering restrictions on its Starshield networks, the military-grade version of SpaceX's Starlink. Ukraine relies on this connectivity to track and intercept incoming threats.
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the U.S. government."
Trump denied on Friday that the White House had ordered restrictions on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces, after Reuters reported on Thursday that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from someone inside the White House, citing two U.S. officials.
The Telegraph reported on Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions.
Additionally, Zelenskyy told NBC's Meet the Press on Sunday that intelligence sharing between the two countries had been interrupted, but later "de-blocked."
Rubio on Monday denied that Washington had suspended intelligence sharing with Ukraine, contradicting Zelenskyy's claim that the flow of information had been briefly interrupted, Reuters reported.
Speaking to reporters in Uzbekistan, Rubio insisted there had been no pause and said Zelenskyy should instead focus on ending the war, marking another public disagreement between Washington and Kyiv amid deteriorating relations.
— CNBC's Lora Kolodny contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: Russian foreign minister says he's visiting Iran for talks to avert return to "large-scale war"
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: Russian foreign minister says he's visiting Iran for talks to avert return to "large-scale war"
articles.content_orig:
Residents of Riyadh, Saudi Arabia's capital city, received alert messages from authorities on Monday that warned of "a hostile aerial threat." AFP journalists received the alerts, too, which were sent to their phones, according to the outlet.
"A warning has been issued by the National Early Warning Platform in Riyadh City to alert of a potential danger," Saudi Arabia's civil defense agency said in a statement on X. The agency also reported that the same warning had been issued for the nearby Kharj area.
A woman in her thirties living in northern Riyadh said she heard the sound of explosions, telling AFP: "we got used to this."
The warning, which often signals incoming Houthi attacks, was lifted shortly after the defense agency's announcement. But it came as attacks by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis have intensified in Saudi Arabia. Hours later, the Houthis claimed a series of missile and drone attacks on Riyadh's international airport and other targets across the kingdom over the past two days.
A major Saudi investment conference has been postponed to next year, its chief executive officer said on Monday, as the kingdom comes under repeated attacks from Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis.
Maha Al Saud, the CEO of the annual Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute, said the event, which was scheduled to take place in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to 29, would instead happen in 2027 in a statement posted on X . She said organizers wanted to ensure the gathering's tenth anniversary edition delivered the "full scale" and "extraordinary quality" participants expected.
"This decision comes from a deep commitment to our partners, members, speakers and delegates," her statement said, adding: "A decade of partnership and shared vision deserves nothing less than our absolute best."
New conference dates will be announced soon, while current registrations and partnerships will remain valid, according to the statement.
For nearly a decade, the conference has served as a showcase for Saudi Arabia's efforts to attract global investors, business leaders and heads of state. The postponement dealt a blow to the kingdom's ambitions to draw foreign capital, diversify its oil-reliant economy and push its reform agenda.
Three sources familiar with the matter had earlier told AFP the conference would be postponed.
Egypt's parliament on Monday postponed its debate on President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi's request to authorize military support to Saudi Arabia, which has faced mounting attacks from Yemen's Houthis, Egyptian state media reported. The debate has been delayed until next week, according to the report.
"House Speaker Hisham Badawi has adjourned the second parliamentary session dedicated to discussing authorisation for taking necessary measures to support and assist the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia, with discussions set to resume on October 26," Egypt's state-run Al-Akhbar newspaper reported.
The postponement concluded a second day of parliamentary sessions in which Egyptian lawmakers weighed Sisi's request to approve support for Saudi Arabia, if requested by the kingdom. An emergency session on Sunday also ended without a decision.
Two lawmakers told AFP on Sunday that most parliamentarians supported the proposal, and a decision wasn't reached during that first session in order to "give all lawmakers the opportunity to speak and express their views."
The Egyptian Social Democratic Party, an opposition party with nearly a dozen seats in parliament, said it had instructed its parliamentary bloc to abstain from voting.
Although it described its solidarity with Saudi Arabia as "firm," the party said any deployment of Egyptian forces abroad should be guided by "specific objectives, clear information" and "an accurate assessment of the potential risks to the lives of our soldiers."
Yemen's Saudi-backed government claimed Monday to have killed 558 Houthi fighters over the past 24 hours. In a post on X , Col. Majed Al-Nazili said Yemeni forces had carried out 1,164 operations against the Iran-backed rebels.
"The operations resulted in neutralizing (558) militia elements, including field commanders," he wrote.
A major Saudi investment conference is set to be postponed, three sources briefed on the matter told the French news agency AFP on Monday, amid repeated attacks on the kingdom by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels .
One source said the event "won't happen on time" and that organizers "won't announce a new date soon." A second source, who confirmed the event would be postponed, told AFP: "Who would be willing to risk flying to Riyadh these days?"
Saudi Arabia's Future Investment Initiative (FII) Institute hosts an annual forum often referred to as "Davos in the desert." The event typically draws foreign leaders and business titans, and this year it is  scheduled to be held in Riyadh from Oct. 26 to 29.
The Wall Street Journal reported that the conference would either be held online or postponed.
Iran's top diplomat on Monday accused the United States of being responsible for the insecurity in the Strait of Hormuz that has left the nearly-eight month conflict sparked by joint U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran unresolved, despite the cessation of major military operations.
"The war imposed by the United States and the Zionist regime [Israel], combined with the economic blockade [on Iran's ports], constitutes the principal source of insecurity in our region," said Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, echoing many similar statements by himself and other senior Iranian figures.
He made the remark Monday during a joint news conference with his Russian counterpart Sergey Lavrov, who arrived in Tehran earlier Monday for his first visit since the outbreak of the war, as Russia tries to frame itself as a potential mediator despite close ties with the Iranian regime.
Lavrov was also scheduled to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian during his visit, according to Russia's foreign ministry. The veteran Russian diplomat said Moscow's efforts were "aimed at preventing the return of a large-scale war," with talks between Tehran and Washington at a standstill.
Iran's Acting Oil Minister Hamid Bovard met Qatar's Minister of State for Energy Affairs, Saad Sherida al-Kaabi, in Doha on Monday to discuss energy relations and cooperation between the two countries.
According to Iran's official news agency IRNA , al-Kaabi confirmed the meeting, which focused on bilateral energy ties and opportunities for cooperation.
The death toll from a Houthi missile strike on a camp in Yemen's government-controlled Shabwa province rose to 50 on Monday, a government official told the French news agency AFP, after military sources earlier put the toll at more than 30.
The Iran-backed rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa.
"The death toll has risen to at least 50, with more than 100 people injured, some of them in critical condition," said Fahad al-Khalifi, deputy governor of Shabwa.
He added that hospitals in the province were overwhelmed and had been forced to transfer the most seriously wounded to facilities in neighbouring Hadramout and Aden.
Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck a military camp for government forces in southern Yemen on Monday, killing at least 20 soldiers, two Yemeni military officials said.
The rebels fired ballistic missiles at the al-Alam military camp in the southern province of Shabwa in an attack that left at least two dozen more troops wounded, the officials said.
The military officials with the internationally recognized government of Yemen spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to brief the media.
Yemen's decade-long civil war has intensified and become intertwined with the wider regional conflict sparked by the U.S. war with Iran over the last few months, as the Houthis, considered one of Iran's most potent proxy forces, attacks the government's Saudi backers on their home turf.

articles.title_orig: Strong Exports Stabilize China’s Economic Growth in Official Statistics
articles.title_zh: Strong Exports Stabilize China’s Economic Growth in Official Statistics
articles.content_orig:
China's economic growth accelerated to 4.5% in the third quarter from a year earlier, as robust foreign demand for the country's technological goods largely offset drags from a deepening property slump and sluggish consumer demand.
Third-quarter growth beat Reuters-polled economists' expectation of a 4.4% expansion, and was also higher than the three-year low of 4.3% in the second quarter .
"The rebound in September salvaged the lukewarm performance in July and August," said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at Economist Intelligence Unit, attributing the recovery to improved government investment that helped arrest the consistent worsening in fixed asset investment, an "ever-strong" external sector and a weak base. China's monthly trade surplus reached a record high of $133.5 billion .
Momentum from the three forces will likely extend into the fourth quarter, Xu said, forecasting a full-year growth rate of 4.7%.
The data shows an economy still leaning on factories and overseas buyers while households and private investors hold back, with growth through the first nine months averaging 4.6%, broadly in line with Beijing's official target range of 4.5% to 5%.
In September, retail sales eked out a 1.1% growth, exceeding analysts' forecast for 0.6% increase, while industrial output grew 5.5% from a year earlier, in line with the forecast of 5.5% growth. The urban unemployment rate stood at 5.2% in September.
For the first nine months this year, fixed asset investment in urban areas declined 7.2% from the same period a year earlier, compared with a 7.3% drop estimated in a Reuters poll. Investment channeled into real estate development deepened declines, falling 20.6% in the January to September period , compared with 19.9% in the first eight months.
"The prolonged housing slump will continue to limit the spillover from stronger industrial activity to the wider economy," Sheana Yue, senior economist at Oxford Economics, as Chinese households see their wealth stored in property shrink over the years.
Yue also dismissed the idea that green shoots have emerged in the property market, as home sales, construction starts, and prices offer little indication that the sector downturn is "bottoming out."
Beijing has leaned heavily on exports for growth this year, but that engine faces growing pressure as energy costs surge and its manufacturing and export surge has provoked growing anxiety among trading partners. Meanwhile, other pockets of the economy remain weak, weighed down by feeble consumption and a multiyear property slump.
"It is clear that domestic imbalances between supply and demand continue rising," Eswar Prasad, an economics professor at Cornell University, said in an emailed note after the data release on Monday. "The government might become more sanguine and maintain a passive approach, rather than infusing stimulus into the economy in tandem with much-needed reforms," he added.
Producer prices climbed at their fastest pace in over four years , rising 5% in September, while consumer inflation remains below 1%, reflecting persistent excess capacity and weak demand that are constraining businesses' pricing power. "This potentially leaves firms to absorb more of the cost shock through lower margins rather than higher selling prices," said Yue.
Economists largely expect the People's Bank of China to hold benchmark lending rates unchanged through this year, leaving fiscal measures to do most of the work.
While the decent growth pace may reduce the immediate pressure for Beijing to ramp up stimulus, Yue expects the implementation of already-announced measures to accelerate, supporting investment and activity in the coming quarters.
Chinese authorities have stepped up fiscal support in recent weeks, including a package of targeted rate cuts and mortgage subsidies in late September. Earlier this month, it also allocated 550 billion yuan of unused debt quota to help ease local government financial strains and bolster infrastructure spending.
Correction: This story has been revised to reflect that quarterly GDP growth was 4.5%.

articles.title_orig: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited
articles.title_zh: Houthi attack kills 53 in biggest single loss of life since Yemen civil war reignited
articles.content_orig:
More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.
Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.
Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.
The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.
The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.
“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”
Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month .
Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.
A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.
Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

articles.title_orig: China Tells UK to ‘Think Twice’ Before Following EU on EV Tariffs
articles.title_zh: China Tells UK to ‘Think Twice’ Before Following EU on EV Tariffs
articles.content_orig:
Beijing warns against ‘discriminatory’ step after France drops opposition to British role in Made in Europe package
No 10 has left the door open to imposing tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles as part of the Made in Europe package, prompting a warning from Beijing that such a move would be “discriminatory”.
Downing Street said on Friday that it would “welcome the objective to have the UK included in the Industrial Accelerator Act” after France dropped its opposition to Britain joining the scheme .
The aim of the rules is to curb subsidised Chinese imports by giving EU-made products preferential treatment, but the UK and others such as Norway are worried about being left at a disadvantage if excluded from the scheme.
The price for joining would be aligning with the EU’s tariffs on Chinese EVs imposed by the bloc in 2024, according to a Franco-German proposal on Thursday night that said the UK would have to dynamically align with EU trade defence measures.
The Chinese embassy in London said it was “firmly opposed to any discriminatory practice involving tariff hikes or restrictive measures on Chinese products”. “We have expressed serious concern to the UK side regarding the reports in question,” it said, adding that “trade protectionism runs counter to WTO rules and market principles”.
This week, the business secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said he would not be coerced into aligning with the EU’s policy.
However, the government has been desperate to be included in the Made in Europe package, fearing billions of pounds of trade in the car industry could be lost if the UK is locked out of supply chains in the EU.
Asked whether the UK accepted it would have to put tariffs on Chinese-made vehicles in order to join Made in Europe, a No 10 spokesperson said it was “premature to speculate” on the terms of any deal with the bloc and there was “still a European process to run”.
They added: “But more broadly, on the principle, the UK obviously has its own trade policy and it keeps all tariffs under review. And we work closely with the British automotive sector to make sure that that approach reflects their best interests.”
Chinese EVs are increasingly popular, with BYD sales up 78% year on year in September, Chery up 660% and the lesser-known Changan up by more than 3,000% in terms of market share.
EU lawmakers are expected to finalise the Industrial Accelerator Act, known as Made in Europe legislation, by the end of the year or early 2027.
But MEPs have already tabled 5,100 amendments, including one embracing the UK and giving Andy Burnham time to secure the deal he wants.
Earlier this week the boss of Mercedes-Benz, Ola Källenius, who is also the president of the European car trade body ACEA, warned that locking the UK out of legislation would amount to a “deliberate choice” by EU leaders to “hurt” the car industry across the bloc.
According to the new Franco-German proposal, there would be “an opt-in to further include European partners who were part of the EU single market as of 1 January 2020”, which includes the UK and Norway.
This would be provided those third countries accepted “dynamic alignment on the EU’s conditions related to third countries’ investments and on relevant EU trade defence measures”.
Tariffs could help UK-based manufacturers by preventing cut-price Chinese models flooding the market but they could also push up prices for consumers and harm British manufacturers trying to sell vehicles to China in the case of an escalating trade war. About 80% of UK-made cars are exported, with more than half going to the EU and 6% to China.
Earlier on Thursday the trade minister, Anas Sarwar, hinted that the UK was minded to align on tariffs. He told Politico the UK and the EU must “work together and act in lockstep” to tackle China’s dominance in the automotive sector.
A car industry source said the EU “has recently shown that it is possible to have a dialogue with the Chinese and get some form of safeguarding in place” without retaliation.
China opposes the expansion of EV tariffs. In the past few months it has made what European Commission officials called “bloodcurdling threats” to launch a trade war over the latest plan to impose quotas on Chinese hybrid cars.
While quotas can be introduced within months under World Trade Organization rules, it could take more than a year to impose tariffs on Chinese cars, with strict processes to be followed, starting with notification of an investigation and followed by evidence-gathering and sharing over alleged harms China might be causing to the British car industry.
Liam Byrne, the Labour chair of the parliamentary business committee, has said imposing tariffs on Chinese EVs would be “a small price to pay” to save the industry in both the UK and the EU.
At a conference in London on Thursday night, he said the UK “urgently needs” a new strategy on China to ensure that British and European manufacturing “does not die”.
Byrne, who has been leading an investigation into the UK’s position on China, was highly critical of the government’s approach, which he believes is naive and based on false hopes that China will change its export policy.
“Our China strategy is simply not where it needs to be. The UK urgently needs a coherent China strategy, which it does not have today,” he said.

articles.title_orig: Masts removed from bomb-laden WWII ship in Thames in bid to avoid explosion
articles.title_zh: Masts removed from bomb-laden WWII ship in Thames in bid to avoid explosion
articles.content_orig:
American warship sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard
A sunken US wartime ship in the Thames estuary holding enough unexploded bombs to devastate a Kent coastal town and send a tidal wave through London has been made slightly safer, ministers have announced.
Engineers have removed the masts of the SS Richard Montgomery – a second world war cargo ship that sank in 1944 with approximately 1,400 tonnes of munitions onboard – without triggering the kind of feared explosion that has kept the wreck under constant guard for decades.
The work was carried out because of concerns that the masts, which had remained visible above the water near Sheerness, could collapse in on the deadly cargo and blow up the ship.
The potential effects of an explosion after 82 years under water have divided expert opinion. Some believe it could cause a small tsunami, throw debris 3km into the air, and “level Sheerness”, according to a New Scientist report in 2004. A government report in 2000 said it was widely accepted it would “put property and the local population at risk”.
The exact contents of the ship’s three holds are unknown but a defence agency report estimated there were almost 300 2,000lb (900kg) blockbuster bombs and more than 2,000 cluster bombs.
Keir Mather, the maritime minister, told the Commons on Monday that work had now been completed, with all three masts successfully removed in “complex project requiring specialist programme, engineering and risk management expertise”.
Mather said that the masts had put “significant load on the structure and their removal has reduced that risk and supports the long-term safe management of the site.”
He said work was completed ahead of schedule and below forecast costs, an estimated £9.5m. The masts have now been delivered to a maritime museum, the Historic Dockyard Chatham, “in recognition of the historic significance of the SS Richard Montgomery and its role in supporting the allied forces’ efforts during world war two”.
The wreck would “continue to be subject to continuous monitoring and control via the established exclusion zone”, he said.
A shipping exclusion zone has long been in place around the SS Montgomery, and since 2025 a no-fly zone has been in place – a development that could have been awkward had Boris Johnson’s proposed Thames estuary airport gone ahead.
Although the risk of an accidental major explosion is now deemed remote, local people have been alarmed by incidents in recent years, including the occasional close proximity of cargo shipping, and a paddleboarder who uploaded pictures to social media of himself leaning on the protruding masts.

articles.title_orig: People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again
articles.title_zh: People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again
articles.content_orig:
Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now.
Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW.
The latest use case for AI? Dumbing down your smart TV to get rid of the bloat. A number of developers and vibe coders have recently been sharing solutions for “vibe-coding” your TV to get rid of sponsored ads, speed up the app launcher, redesign the home screen, disable tracking features, and more.
One such solution, called “dumbtv,” describes its mission on its GitHub page thus: “Your TV should do what you paid for: your apps, your HDMI inputs, and nothing else. No ads from the TV itself, no watch tracking, no update you did not ask for.”
Another, “ cleanyourtv ,” promises to strip the bloatware from any Android TV or Google TV over Wi-Fi, to replace the launcher with one that resembles Apple TV.
While hacking consumer electronics devices to gain more control over their systems is hardly a new idea, the latest advances in AI technology have made such efforts much more accessible to anyone. With smart TVs in particular, the hacks come at a time when people have grown frustrated with being forced to watch ads and put up with their devices surveilling their viewing habits.
Modern smart TVs ship with a technology called Automatic Content Recognition (ACR), which identifies what’s playing on the screen using screenshots, audio clips or other forms of digital fingerprinting.
If these “dumb TV” hacks become more popular among everyday consumers, they have the potential to disrupt the smart TV ad industry, which profits from selling viewing data to advertisers or using it to display personalized ads on their own interfaces.
As the creator of cleanyourtv, Gathin T., puts it, the idea to clean up the smart TV interface started one afternoon when he got tired of seeing the ads on his parents’ TV set.
Vibe coded my parents' TV this afternoon! It was showing a sponsored ad before you could even get to Netflix. Gave Claude Code the model number, it found the TV on wifi, removed 25 Xiaomi packages and wrote a new launcher. Looks like an Apple TV now lol pic.twitter.com/E5Q4A1b0yI
“I had Claude Code clean it up over Wi-Fi and build a simple home screen with just their apps on it. I put the prompt on GitHub, tweeted the before and after,s and a few thousand people did the same to their own TVs over the next two days. Xiaomi, TCL, Sony, Fire TV, LG, a projector or two,” the developer wrote on a website for donations, linked from the project’s homepage .
The solution doesn’t require gaining root access to the TV, nor does it make it impossible to return to the factory default state, if desired.
Meanwhile, the dumbtv solution has been tested end-to-end on a Fire TV Edition television set and Android/Google TV platforms on TVs from Sony, TCL, Philips, Hisense, Xiaomi, and Shield. To use this hack, the developer, Muzammil Yasin Sabuwala, suggests pointing your preferred AI agent at the dumbtv repository on GitHub.
Sabuwala said he was motivated to work on dumbtv because he was tired of the ads and not being able to delve directly into the content he wanted to watch. His solution was coded using a combination of Deepseek V4.1 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, he told TechCrunch, and he plans to maintain the GitHub, adding support for more models over time.
introducing dumbtv – no spying – no ads from tv – fully customisable to setup just point your agent to this repo – https://t.co/prQLD17Wa4 https://t.co/z41SWJZVXt pic.twitter.com/c6R8EhljiA
Fair warning: all these solutions are works in progress, and various users are now testing them across different TV platforms and suggesting updates and fixes.
However, individuals don’t need to borrow someone else’s work from GitHub to get the job done.
In one newly viral X post, Ryan Doyle explains that he simply sent Claude Code the listing for his TV and asked “Can you hack this?” The agent then talked him through the process, allowing him to remove the ads and bloatware from the TV set, speed up the lagging user interface, and customize his screensaver, he claims.
Doyle then goes on to demonstrate in a video how fast and responsive the new interface is after the AI made the requested changes.
This is how fast the TV moves now that Claude deleted all the BS laggy bloatware it comes with https://t.co/nUCEjqPwAO pic.twitter.com/g07CEgC1GJ
Seeing posts about people “vibe-coding their TVs,” inspired one X user, Mihir Gupta, to try it himself.
“One afternoon with Claude Code: 25 bloat apps disabled, the 192 MB stock launcher replaced with a custom 83 MB one, plus rotating wallpapers,” he wrote .
The end result of these hacks may be mixed, however. Some people have found that Claude wouldn’t respond to their simple suggestions to “hack my TV,” necessitating more complex prompts. Others warned that AI agents could make mistakes, possibly disabling important packages or breaking things in the process. One person even said they bricked their Android TV using Claude , and another got stuck halfway through hacking their Fire TV.
For those wary of using AI to fully hack their TVs, there are existing solutions for customizing Android-based smart TVs, such as home screen replacement apps ATV Launcher, Projectivity Launcher, and FLauncher.

articles.title_orig: Musk Vows to Give Each U.S. Child a SpaceX Share
articles.title_zh: Musk Vows to Give Each U.S. Child a SpaceX Share
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said Monday that he'll give every child in the U.S. one of his shares in the company next year.
Musk currently owns about 4.8 billion SpaceX shares, according to an August SEC filing. That figure rises to 6.4 billion when taking into account unvested awards and stock options, representing a 48.4% beneficial stake in the company.
There were 72 million children under 18 in the U.S. as of July 1, 2025, according to official census data.
That would amount to the CEO giving away about $10.5 billion worth of shares, taking into account SpaceX's closing stock price of $146.03 as of Friday.
"This will be the first of many," Musk said in a post on X, without providing further details on how the share giveaway would happen.
CNBC has reached out to SpaceX and Musk's family office for further details.
Altimeter Capital's Brad Gerstner, founder of Invest America and Trump Accounts, praised the move and suggested in a post on X that the SpaceX shares could be distributed via Trump accounts.
"Incredible Elon!" he wrote. "This will be the largest philanthropic gift in history! 70 M accounts - every citizen under 18 & every child born forevermore now has a free, lifetime investment acct making them an owner in the upside of America & our greatest companies!"
Musk's financial giving has been in the news in recent weeks primarily for his political contributions.
The Tesla CEO has spent more than $276 million in donations to Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election.
The world's richest person poured $158 million into the Senate Leadership Fund, the Republican Party's leading Senate super PAC, in September through an affiliated Texas PAC created to support Republican Ken Paxton. Musk's two contributions of $75 million and $83 million are among the largest political donations ever.
When it comes to fulfilling his philanthropic promises , Musk has a spotty track record.
For example, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO contributed about $38 million to OpenAI , which he co-founded as a nonprofit research lab, between 2016 and 2020. But he had promised to contribute up to $1 billion, and cut off donations to the organization amid a battle with cofounders for control of the company.
In 2021, Musk said he would donate $6 billion to the United Nations World Food Program if it could show him a plan for how they'd use the money to "solve world hunger." While the WFP posted a plan , Musk did not donate.
Musk's foundation has also repeatedly fallen shy of making the minimum donations it's required to by law, and as The New York Times previously reported, its donations go to charities that closely benefit Musk and his companies directly.
Musk's post came just after Anthropic revealed plans to commit 5% of its shares to a new public benefit fund, with the stake potentially increasing as the company's valuation grows.
In response to an Anthropic post on X about the fund on Sunday, Musk replied, "I recommend giving the shares directly to the public," and added that's what he'd be doing.
Subject to shareholder approval, Anthropic's fund would immediately commit 5% of Anthropic's shares, with the board adding, at its discretion, an additional 2% for every 50% increase in the company's value above a set baseline that has yet to be disclosed.
The fund may be used to "explore large donations," including to traditional nonprofits or as direct distributions for specific populations, or for "bolder approaches" to study and address AI's disruption and displacement of jobs, the company said.
— CNBC's Jennifer Liu contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Amazon stock pops after Morgan Stanley details 5 catalysts, lifts price target
articles.title_zh: Amazon stock pops after Morgan Stanley details 5 catalysts, lifts price target
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Amazon ( AMZN ) stock rose as much as 5% on Monday after Morgan Stanley named it a top pick and raised its price target to $350 from $335, outlining five catalysts that could drive the stock higher.
The new target implies about 40% upside from Friday's close of $250. With a bear case of $220 a share and a bull case of $410, the firm sees a 3:1 risk-reward ratio.
"In a market of see-sawing AI leaders and laggards, we detail 5 catalysts ahead to re-rate shares and drive material outperformance," analyst Brian Nowak, who kept his Overweight rating, wrote in a note Sunday.
Faster AWS growth: Morgan Stanley now expects revenue at AWS, Amazon's cloud unit, to grow 47% in 2027 and 42% in 2028, up from 41% and 37%. The change follows Nvidia's ( NVDA ) disclosure that it expects AWS to buy and deploy about 2 million of its GPUs over those two years. The extra chips also lift the firm's capital spending forecast for Amazon to $355 billion in 2027 and $365 billion in 2028.
Bigger AWS profits: Nowak expects AWS operating margins of 42% in 2027 and 44% in 2028, which supports about $16.50 in Amazon earnings per share in 2028.
Bedrock: More visibility into Bedrock, Amazon's AI model service, could lift the stock's valuation from about 15 times 2028 earnings, according to the note.
AI shopping: Nowak expects Amazon to emerge as a winner as AI shopping agents spread and expects it to partner over time with Meta's ( META ) Muse AI agent . The holiday season is the first big test.
Robotics: Every 10% of Amazon's global units that move through its robotics-enabled fulfillment centers could save $2 billion to $4 billion a year, Morgan Stanley estimates. The firm calls robotics a 2027 catalyst.
Amazon stock is up about 11% this year but sits roughly 10% below its early August high. Earlier this month, Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi noted that Amazon was trading at one of its lowest trailing price-to-earnings ratios in years . Morgan Stanley's $350 target is based on about 21 times its 2028 earnings estimate.
Amazon reports third quarter results on Oct. 29 after the bell.

articles.title_orig: Tehran seeks to punish Trump in midterms with oil price pain, Iranian officials say
articles.title_zh: Tehran seeks to punish Trump in midterms with oil price pain, Iranian officials say
articles.content_orig:
At least 15 vessels struck in waterway in past 10 days, with rumours that they were carrying valuable goods
People have been scouring the strait of Hormuz for spilt cargo after Iran attacked at least 15 container ships passing through the crucial waterway in the past 10 days.
Some ships have been hit by drones, others by mines. On Sunday, a ship was struck by a rocket-propelled grenade launched from a small boat 75 miles (120km) north-east of the Saudi port of Jubail.
The rise in Iranian attacks appears to have helped resolidify Tehran’s disputed control over the strait, as well as pushing the price of a barrel of Brent crude oil close to $108 a barrel on Monday morning.
Last Wednesday a ship travelling from Karachi, Pakistan, to Fujairah, in the United Arab Emirates , sunk after hitting a mine, according to Iranian state TV. All 21 crew members were evacuated and no injuries were reported. Dozens of its 2,500 containers were seen floating in the water. Rumours that iPhones and other expensive goods were among its cargo – fuelled by fake AI-generated photos published on social media – prompted fishers and others to investigate.
One fisher told an Iranian reporter: “The Arab boatmen, who were closer to the ship, arrived earlier than the Iranians. They used stonecutters to cut the container and took whatever was there.”
Col Javad Mokhtar Rezaei, the deputy head of cultural and social affairs for Iran’s cyber police (Fata), told the Tasnim news agency: “In some cases, the phones offered may actually exist, but exposing electronic components to salt water and extreme humidity can cause corrosion of internal components, damage to the boards, battery and display, and cause hidden malfunctions in the device’s performance.”
Meysam Doost-Mohammadi, a spokesperson for the Iranian mobile phone Aassociation, said it would be unusual for valuable devices to be transported by ship.
The bulk of the recent attacks have occurred close to the coast with Oman , a route that Iran regards as unauthorised. In the seven days to Friday 16 October, 12 vessels were attacked, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations Centre (UKMTO).
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps ( IRGC) says it has the right to attack any ship that seeks to traverse the strait without its permission or with its transponders off. Officials have also ordered local fishers not to pillage the sea for luxury items, saying the goods are the property of the state.
Two oil tankers were hit on Saturday, including a supertanker carrying 2m barrels of oil, according to the IRGC. The Fars news agency published a video that appears to show the tanker burning, but which cannot be independently verified. A third tanker was hit late on Sunday.
It is disputed how many ships have been hit by mines or IRGC shelling. UKMTO’s weekly overview recorded 254 transits of the strait (125 outbound, 129 inbound) in the week to 14 October, approximately 70% below pre-conflict levels.
Dr Devaraj Asir Ramesh, of Anna University in Chennai, India, warned that the region’s marine habitats faced threats from toxic debris and oil spills, while noise might have disturbed marine life. Iranian strikes on the Emirates, he said, were likely to have contaminated seagrass beds with hydrocarbons and caused auditory damage to cetaceans – marine mammals such as dolphins and porpoises – which are sensitive to loud noise that travels through the sea.
Oil released by attacks on tankers at Fujairah could have caused ecological harm, he added. “Oil spills, chemical leaks and acoustic disturbances have impaired biodiversity, fisheries, aquaculture, desalination, and eco-tourism,” he wrote in the International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Sciences.
On Friday, the Iranian president said the conflicts in Gaza and the wider Middle East had inflicted a significant toll on nature that extended beyond borders and required “international solutions”.
“What has occurred in our region as a result of wars of aggression is ecocide, or environmental genocide, and it must be condemned,” Masoud Pezeshkian said. He argued that countries subjected to economic sanctions or military aggression should not be forced to shoulder the financial burden of environmental damage resulting from conflicts they did not initiate.
Successive studies, mainly by US universities using satellite imagery, have warned of the dangers facing the strait.
Meanwhile, the Russian foreign minister, Sergei Lavrov, visited Tehran offering to act as an intermediary between Iran and Donald Trump, especially over the issue of Iran’s nuclear stockpile, which the US president insists must be addressed before he lifts his threat to attack Iran again.
Iran has offered to open the strait in six days in return for sanctions relief.
Russia has offered to take Iran’s stockpile of highly enriched uranium, but Iran is reluctant to make a commitment on its nuclear programme and has not given the International Atomic Energy Agency access to its bombed nuclear sites since June 2025. Lavrov also proposed a trilateral summit between China, Russia and Iran to agree new security architecture for the strait. He said the region was on the verge of a full-scale crisis.
Tehran is braced for another attack soon, especially after the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, launched a new national security doctrine on Sunday that included an emphasis on prevention and offence, including pre-emptive strikes on potential threats.

articles.title_orig: Agencies flouting China travel ban, sources say
articles.title_zh: Agencies flouting China travel ban, sources say
articles.content_orig:
Some travel agencies are using labels such as “cultural visits” to advertise tours to China despite the government’s ban on organized group travel, sources from the tourism industry said on Sunday.
The number of Taiwanese traveling to China rose 19.63 percent year-on-year to 2.49 million in the first eight months of this year, making China the second-most popular overseas destination, after Japan.
Taiwan has maintained the ban since February 2024, allowing only independent trips to China. However, sources told the Chinese-language Liberty Times (the sister paper of the Taipei Times) that travel agencies are advertising China tour packages under labels such as “cultural visits” and “group independent travel.”
Taiwan first banned travel agencies from organizing outbound tours in 2020 in response to the COVID-19 pandemic. The ban was scheduled to be lifted in 2024, but Taipei maintained the restrictions in response to Beijing’s prohibition on Chinese tour groups and independent travelers visiting Taiwan.
Statistics released by the Tourism Administration on Saturday show that Taiwanese made 14.53 million overseas trips from January through August, including 2.49 million to China, accounting for 17.4 percent of the total. Commenting on the increase, Providence University Department of Tourism associate professor Huang Cheng-tsung (黃正聰) said the increase in travel to China was consistent with the overall growth in overseas travel.
Meanwhile, sources told the Liberty Times that travel agencies were advertising itineraries to popular Chinese destinations, including Jiuzhaigou, Xinjiang, Zhangjiajie and the Yangtze River. The Web sites listed daily itineraries resembling conventional group tours, but marketed them as cultural visits or group independent travel.
However, in practice, agencies were dispatching their staff to accompany travelers, potentially violating the restrictions, they said.
When reached for comment on Sunday, Tourism Administration Deputy Director-General Huang Ho-ting (黃荷婷) said that travel agencies remain prohibited from openly soliciting members of the public to join organized tours to China. Violators face fines of up to NT$50,000 under the Regulations Governing Travel Agencies (旅行業管理規則).
An industry source who spoke on condition of anonymity said a common workaround was for associations, community groups, village and borough wardens, businesses, government agencies, or groups of friends and relatives to organize their own trips and hire travel agencies to handle the arrangements.
The source cited a bus crash involving a group of relatives and friends traveling in Gansu Province this year as an example.
Another method involves travelers departing Taiwan separately as independent travelers, then gathering in China to join an organized tour. This allows some agencies to continue recruiting participants discreetly despite the ban, the source said.
“For travel agencies, it is a strange rule that does little damage, but is deeply insulting,” the source said.
Travel Association of Chinese chairman Hsu Chin-ruey (許晉睿) said agencies might legitimately post tourism information on their Web sites for reference, provided listings do not include departure dates or indicate that trips are open for registration.
Such information might fall within the normal scope of a travel agency’s business, he said.
However, members of the public who find Web sites listing departure dates and opening registrations can report them to the Tourism Administration.
Huang said agencies may still organize visits and inspection tours, arrange trips organized by groups themselves, and book plane tickets and accommodation for travelers heading to China.
Exchange or inspection delegations invited by Chinese organizations are exempt from the suspension if they have specific purposes, designated destinations and eligibility requirements for participants, she said.
She urged agencies to comply with the rules and avoid illegally soliciting customers, which could lead to travel disputes.
If the Tourism Administration confirms that an agency has illegally solicited participants for an organized tour to China, it can order the agency to make improvements by a specified deadline or impose a fine of NT$10,000 to NT$50,000, Huang said.

articles.title_orig: Explainer: What's behind Egypt's move towards possible military involvement in Saudi-Yemen conflict?
articles.title_zh: Explainer: What's behind Egypt's move towards possible military involvement in Saudi-Yemen conflict?
articles.content_orig:
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi has requested emergency parliamentary approval to defend Saudi Arabia against escalating attacks by Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthi rebels.
The announcement follows military assistance from Pakistan and Turkey, which have deployed personnel, equipment and other defensive resources to support Saudi Arabia amid renewed fighting in Yemen.
Speaking at a graduation ceremony at the Egyptian Military Academy on Saturday , October 17, al-Sisi said Egypt was prepared to intervene if requested by Saudi Arabia, but stressed that any action would require parliamentary approval.
“I call on parliament to convene an emergency session to authorise us to take action to intervene in defence of Saudi Arabia, if we are asked to do so,” he said.
“This move and this defence require approval from the Egyptian parliament. I hope parliament will convene an emergency session to grant this authorisation.
"I am not speaking about attacking or waging war. We are seeking only to defend.”
Egypt's House of Representatives subsequently scheduled an emergency session for Sunday, October 18, in response to the president's request.
The announcement comes amid renewed missile and drone attacks by the Houthis on Saudi infrastructure, including Riyadh's international airport and facilities belonging to state oil company Saudi Aramco.
Fighting intensified after a truce in Yemen collapsed , with Saudi-backed forces launching a fresh campaign against the Houthis, who control significant territory in the country.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi reaffirmed his country's commitment to defending Saudi Arabia, warning against threats to Red Sea security and international shipping lanes while stressing that Cairo would not stand aside if the kingdom faced further attacks.
"I want to tell the whole world that we are not looking for a role to play, but it is absolutely unacceptable for us to allow the kingdom of Saudi Arabia to be targeted or for its security and stability to be undermined," he added.
Egypt's announcement comes as Pakistan and Turkey strengthen defence cooperation with Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed on August 7, 2026, which treats an armed attack against one member as an attack against all three.
Pakistan has deployed military personnel and resources to Saudi Arabia , with its Foreign Ministry confirming on October 9 that their role was defensive and did not involve operations inside Yemen.
Turkey has also provided air defence systems, intelligence support, drone operators and logistics, according to Reuters . President Recep Tayyip Erdogan announced on October 12 that he would submit the agreement to parliament for ratification.
Earlier in October, officials from the three countries met in Riyadh and agreed to coordinate military resources to strengthen Saudi Arabia's security against Houthi attacks.
Neither Pakistan nor Turkey has confirmed deploying combat troops into Yemen, with their reported assistance focused on defending Saudi territory.
The developments coincide with Egypt's consideration of joining the Mecca defence alliance, with Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty confirming on October 13 that Cairo was examining membership but had yet to make a final decision.

articles.content_orig:
More than 200 mostly young people said to be injured after ballistic missile attack on training camp for government forces
At least 53 people have been killed in a Houthi ballistic missile attack on a training camp for Yemeni government security forces, making it the largest single loss of life since the country’s civil war reignited in September.
The attack on al-Alam camp in the southern Shabwa province was said to have injured more than 200 others, mostly young recruits, and was described as a disaster by the country’s UN-recognised government. The injured were taken from the police and army training camp in the Jardan district to a hospital in the local capital, Ataq, where pleas for blood donations were made.
There will be an inquiry into how so many troops were left so exposed to a Houthi attack. In mid-September, the group began a fresh push on forces backing the UN-recognised government by pushing south along the Red Sea coast to try to take control of the Bab al-Mandab waterway.
Reliable assessments of the death toll in the fighting over the last month are hard to gather, but it is running into the many thousands. A Saudi airstrike on Sunday killed nine, including five children and two women.
Rashad al-Alimi, the president of the UN-recognised government, said those killed on Monday were new recruits, and he vowed an immediate hard response. He said the incident “affirmed that targeting the recruits reflects the Houthi militias’ approach of resorting to cowardly terrorist attacks whenever they face pressures or their Iranian-backed sabotage plots falter”.
On Monday he phoned the UN secretary general, António Guterres, to ask for the UN to classify the Houthis as a foreign terrorist organisation.
The Shabwa provincial authority said: “Targeting recruits constitutes a military escalation and a blatant assault on the province’s security.” Its governor, Awad bin al-Wazir, visited the wounded in hospitals, and called for extra air defences, saying troops were fighting across six fronts.
The killings underline the dangers of large numbers of troops gathering in one place within reach of the Houthi ballistic missile arsenal. The training camp was struck by three ballistic missiles while the recruits lined up in formation.
Houthi forces have also cut the road between government-run Shabwa and the Houthi-run Bayda governorate.
The Houthi military spokesperson said: “Our armed forces targeted the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations in al-Alam camp, which is run by Saudi officers in the eastern regions. The targeting resulted in the fall of dozens of dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations, including Saudi officers.
“We warn the deceived ones against responding to the Saudi enemy’s calls to lure them with his defiled money to the pyres of death, and to exploit them instead of his soldiers who are indifferent to their lives.”
A Yemen government spokesperson said the site struck was not a military target linked to the current fighting but “a training centre where new recruits in the internal security forces of Shabwa governorate receive training and qualification programmes.”
They added: “This reveals the criminal nature of this assault, which targeted young people in the preparation and qualification phase to carry out their security duties, far from the frontlines.”
Separately the Houthis claim to have hit the anti-Houthi Giant Brigades of southern Yemen in six strikes in the areas of al-Suqya and Ras al-Ara. Southern forces are said to have been making progress in edging Houthi forces out of control of the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, the narrowest waterway taking ships from the Red Sea to the Indian Ocean.
Fighting is also under way as Houthis try to mount a siege of Taiz, where citizens have been calling for greater air protection. In the city there seems to be a determination not to capitulate, but conditions are deteriorating as Houthis close access points.
It is not clear whether the Houthis have decided to slow the pace of attacks on Saudi airports and energy installations, or they are running low on munitions.
The Saudi Aramco headquarters was struck last weekend and some airlines have said they will not yet resume using Riyadh airport. The airport reopened at the weekend after being attacked this month .
Egypt’s parliament has postponed a vote on whether to send troops to Saudi Arabia despite extending the debate to a second day as MPs demanded more than two minutes each to speak. The vote is now likely to be held next week.
A two-thirds majority is required, and some opposition parties have signalled their intention to vote against or abstain. Disputes centre on the extent of the mission and whether it will involve sending troops into Yemen to help Saudi Arabia, and whether Egyptian troops inside Saudi Arabia would become targets for Houthi attacks.
The delay also gives the Egyptians time to see if Iran can persuade the Houthis to hold back, and for Saudi Arabia to confirm the renewal of badly needed loans to Egypt.
Egypt has resisted any ground intervention in Yemen, dating back to the 1962-67 war, when Gamal Abdel Nasser sent troops to back the republicans in North Yemen against the Saudi- and British-backed royalists. The incursion was intended to be minimal, but escalated to as many as 70,000 soldiers. Estimates of Egyptians killed range from 10,000-26,000.

articles.title_orig: The AI doom scenario you've never heard of may be the hardest to stop
articles.title_zh: The AI doom scenario you've never heard of may be the hardest to stop
articles.content_orig:
It seems that almost daily, a big tech company releases a new AI-driven digital assistant. Muse by Meta, Gemini by Google, dots by OpenAI. By the time this article is published, a new one from [insert tech company here] will probably have a press release touting its ability to manage your work and life — to take things off your plate, automate your processes, speed up your tedious tasks. It sounds helpful and, to lower the bar, harmless.
But some researchers say this is the beginning of a treacherous path for humankind, one where bots take more and more off our plate until all that's left is an empty vessel, and we human users become nothing more than thoughtless "approvers."
It's not just a threat to jobs . They warn that  allowing our skills and knowledge to deteriorate, and surrendering our critical thinking to AI, poses an existential danger to humanity.
One term for this path is "gradual disempowerment" — a scenario where AI displaces human labor in the economy, replaces human decision-making in all key societal concerns, erodes human creativity, and degrades human cognition along the way.
And though the word "gradual" is in the name, that does not mean the problem is something to worry about far in the future, according to experts.
"I put gradual disempowerment on the very top of my list," said Jay Chooi, the founder and CEO of Robocurve, a company that tracks and measures AI-driven robotics capabilities.
Chooi believes gradual disempowerment is just as worrisome as the threat of engineered pandemics and more destructive cyberattacks , which could be accelerated by capable AI.
"It's a civilization-scale problem," Chooi said of gradual disempowerment. "A lot of people feel very powerless, because it requires a lot of effort and a whole-of-society approach to solve it."
The term "gradual disempowerment" stems from a paper published in early 2025.
At the heart of the gradual disempowerment scenario is AI technology continuing to advance in capabilities, as it has rapidly since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022.
AI models may soon be better at nearly all cognitive tasks than humans — solving frontier math problems , doing hard science, coding, writing and creating art and music, to name a few of the areas where AI increasingly excels. At the same time, advances in robotics could lead to AI-powered robots performing better than humans at physical labor like packing boxes, constructing homes, building cars, painting murals, mining for rare minerals, and even building IKEA furniture .
We like to think that in an ideal world, the best applicant generally gets the job, and they are paid based on the level of demand for their skills. But imagine if a human is never the best person for the job. That's a world that some AI prognosticators and whistleblowers expect.
It's a world where an AI agent or AI-enabled robot is better at every task and sub-task that it takes to do my job and your job. They move faster than us, think deeper, have more patience and stamina. They more cordially answer phones, do more thorough research, and more dexterously wield a scalpel or a nail file. Plus, they never need to sleep or take sick days, they never show up hungover or moody, and they never threaten to leave for a better job.
To picture gradual disempowerment more clearly, here's a scenario: Let's say you run Hammer Co., a company that manufactures hammers. You have line workers who shape the steel heads and wooden handles and then fit them together, and managers who keep the factory running smoothly. You have people who maintain your supply chain and teams to handle marketing, sales, accounting, and all the other functions that help your business thrive.
But then a tech company comes out with AI-powered Hammer Bots. The robot workers can make hammers far faster than your human workers, while AI agents can run the business side with little oversight. They'll work all night, never make mistakes, and cost far less than your happy, well-paid staff. You don't want to fire your human workers. You see them around town and have known their families for years, after all.
But your competitor gets the Hammer Bots. Most customers just want the cheapest hammers — they don't care who or what makes them. As CEO of Hammer Co. you either compete or die. So you fire all your humans and get Hammer Bots to replace them.
Now, try to envision this is the case for every company, and every job. With normal free-market incentives, the company that stays loyal to its human employees will be outcompeted by the company that gets AI to do the work instead.
Here's where gradual disempowerment comes into play.
The fewer humans that participate in labor, and the more work that's outsourced to AI agents, the more humanity becomes dependent on AI for decision-making and the more human skills deteriorate. How long until  the finer points of hammer-making will be forgotten?
With AI making all our complex decisions for us, humans become less capable of understanding and overseeing those decisions or of pushing back against them.
"If people aren't actually practicing the skills that the agents are doing for them, they lose the ability to have that skill, and so now you become reliant," said Margaret Mitchell, an AI research scientist at Hugging Face and co-author of another recent paper on the importance of keeping humans in the loop in an AI world.
"What happens when something goes wrong? There's no human you can point to who can fix it. So now you've become fully dependent on these systems to fix themselves, and what if that's not possible?"
It's not just economics and labor at risk. Take the military , for example. All or most decisions in war involve humans today, even if AI contributes to the process, but the balance is likely to shift as the technology becomes more capable.
If the United States uses AI to make decisions in battle , its enemies across the field will be pressured to do the same. The side that leans more heavily on humans will be slower and less efficient. Human soldiers need food and rest. Robot soldiers will not. Human decision-makers are limited in the scenarios they can conceive and plan for; AIs can take into account all of human knowledge.
"The states need citizens. They need us because we pay taxes and we fight for the states in the military," said Jan Kulveit, a co-author of the gradual disempowerment paper and co-founder of ACS Research Group.
States also use people to enforce laws. But what if law enforcement is all automated in the future?
"If, or when, existing states don't need their citizens, they're less likely to be democratic," said Kulveit.
Kulveit compares theoretical future countries that are mostly run by AI to oil states today. He said the oil states tend to be authoritarian because they don't rely on most of their citizens to pay taxes and don't need citizens' votes to rule. States that rely on AI to run the economy and military could have similar outcomes, said Kulveit.
If that is the case, and citizens no longer are the backbone of labor or warfare in a world of gradual disempowerment, then humans lose perhaps their greatest leverage against those in power.
"A lot of people are talking about rogue AI hacking into data centers and taking over the world, but it is not in the mainstream consciousness that like AI could literally take over the world just by continuing to do what it's supposed to do, which is automating everything," said Jay Chooi of Robocurve.
"Organizations are all going to have a very strong economic pressure, and political pressure, to phase out humans and move work more and more into robots or AI."
Humans ceding control to AI, say the gradual disempowerment authors, is almost a natural transition once very advanced AI is here.
Gradual disempowerment "does not need to emerge from a deliberate scheme or powergrab by AI systems," wrote Kulveit and his colleagues. "In the short-term, it is being incentivized by the perceived value that AI systems can b

articles.title_orig: Unprecedented Collab Between China and the Met Uncovers Secrets of Chinese Mural During Exhaustive Reproduction
articles.title_zh: Unprecedented Collab Between China and the Met Uncovers Secrets of Chinese Mural During Exhaustive Reproduction
articles.content_orig:
A major arts and heritage conservation project in China has born unexpected fruit thousands of miles away in New York City.
In the Chinese arts and antiquities gallery of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, a 50-foot-long mural devours the attention of an entire room with its arrangement of Buddha and his attendants.
The Medicine Buddha mural had long attracted the wonder of Zhang Jian, director of the “Meticulous Painting Institute” at the Chinese National Academy of Arts, which since 2013 has poured billions of Chinese RMB into restoring, conserving, and repatriating Chinese artifacts around the country and the world.
Describing it as wielding an “awe-inspiring energy,” Zhang learned that the mural was originally located in the ancient Guangsheng Temple in central China. Standing in its halls years later, staring at the vacant space where the massive mural had originally hung, Zhang was struck with an idea.
Over the next 3 years, he led a team of special artists and conservationists to the Met to meticulously—excruciatingly—copy the mural for a life-sized replica that captures every single crack, faded contour, and conservationist correction it had faced in its 700 years on the Earth.
This project was made possible with the unerring support of the Met itself, a collaboration which marks arguably the highest ever undertaken between Chinese and American cultural institutes.
Now in October, the Met is to co-host an international symposium in Beijing about Chinese murals, marking the first time the New York museum has jointly held a major academic conference in China with a national research body.
Jason Sun, the Met’s curator of Chinese art, told the South China Morning Post that the results achieved by Zhang’s team—including the realization that conservators had incorrectly arranged the mural segments so that Lord Buddha’s head was 2 centimeters off kilter—as having “profound historical and practical significance.”
Painted around 700 years ago during the Mongol-administered Yuan Dynasty, on clay tiles mixed with rice straw, the mural depicts the Medicine Buddha seated with his chief attendants surrounded by numerous figures.
Yet its presence in the Met isn’t the result of it being a plundered relic. Mainland China was mostly free from Western colonial occupation when the impoverished monks from Guangsheng Temple chopped the mural up into sections and sold it to fix the collapsing roof of their temple.
Among the keystones of Buddha’s teachings is the unavoidable truth that all things are impermanent, so if they were good students of the Great Sage, those impoverished monks would not have hesitated to part with the relic, that traded hands across the West until it arrived at the Met via donation from Arthur Sackler in 1965.
The China National Arts Fund, a state-endowed philanthropic fund established in 2013 under the National Academy of Arts, was as recently as 2025 tasked specifically with the preservation of ancient murals and other works. So far, 40 ancient murals from caves and temples across Western China have been painstakingly examined and copied, but if they are held overseas, the Fund has the directive to pay for their study, and potentially, their recreation.
Yet Zhang had a different sort of intention for that recreation: one that the Met administrators enthusiastically supported. In 2024, SCMP reports that the Fund had formalized a research partnership with the Met, whereby the famous museum granted their colleagues in East Asia full authorization for prolonged detailed study of the work, and the sharing of ultra-high-resolution digital images.
CHINESE MURALS IN THE NEWS: Stunning Tang Dynasty Mural Unearthed in China Portrays a ‘Westerner’ with Blonde Hair
“The Met staff actively coordinated with visitors for us,” said Meng Ying, an artist on Zhang’s team which visited the Met 3 times over the following years. “Though our lifts and lighting equipment occasionally blocked sightlines, visitors were remarkably understanding.”
As Meng said, studying portions of the work required specialized hydraulic lifts and expansive light fixtures, conditions which he described as being “unprecedented” in the history of the Met. This went on for days at a time, while the team poured their attention onto the smallest details to reproduce exactly what it was that the Guangsheng Temple was missing.
This included using clay-rich mud and rice straw to make the tiles, which they sourced from as close to the temple as possible. It involved extensive studying into the mineral pigments—considering what would have been available to the medieval painters, and how such materials could have changed over 700 years.
“Lighting, digital cameras ,and printing all change how a color looks. We had to tweak our paints over and over again on site,” said Han Maoyuan, another artist on the team.
MORE COLLABORATION LIKE THIS: Since 1968 French Teachers Have Come to Louisiana Classrooms to Preserve French Language Through Immersion
Yet further, the team layered their mud tiles to create a base-layer painting and a second to replicate the scars left by time and intervention.
As mentioned earlier, the team’s exhaustive examination of the mural revealed that its original mounters in the Met’s galleries had misunderstood Chinese brushwork, and misaligned the Buddha’s head by 2 centimeters. Met staff told SCMP that after the disbelief wore off, they couldn’t walk through the room without noticing that the Buddha’s head was crooked.
The finished mural produced by Zhang and his team made its public debut at the China National Arts and Crafts Museum in Beijing, where on September 24th, in honor of President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US, an exhibition was held featuring the fruits of the National Art Fund’s preservation and reproduction efforts.
FROM THE MET: Rare Chinese ‘Magic Mirror’ That Projects Hidden Image Rediscovered After Decades in Museum Storage
Zhang said it would allow this ancient mural to re-enter contemporary cultural life, yet with all the context that great works of art carry with them as the centuries load up on their shoulders.
Other murals from Guangsheng, as it turns out, are located in American Museums—in Cincinnati and Missouri—both have which have already contacted Zhang for the purpose of examining the alignments and conditions of the works.
